relation_to_previous: Independent of v1 and v2, which are unchanged on disk. Benchmark v2's held-out split has been used (its results were observed) and must no longer be described as untouched. This v3 set is a fresh final held-out set for the Milestone 11C comparison. No question here duplicates a v1 or v2 question.
description: 30 scored retrieval cases and 6 behaviour cases over the pinned 23-record MITRE subset (CWE 4.20 and CAPEC 3.9). A SMALL, MANUALLY AUTHORED benchmark: it is not an unbiased or comprehensive relevance assessment and is not evidence of general retrieval quality.
protocol: All cases are the final held-out set. They must be run only after the retriever implementation, embedding model and revision, and configuration are frozen, and never used for tuning. Defects found after retrieval has been observed must not be fixed in place: document the defect and create a new benchmark version. See evaluation_protocol_11c.md.
annotation_guide: data/retrieval_benchmark/ANNOTATION_GUIDE_v2.md (relevance rules 1-2 and the conjunction rule) with the v3 differences listed in label_method

label_method.summary: Single pass by the authoring AI assistant, from the source text of the records only. Each relevant label cites a verbatim quote from the record and section that supports it; records that were considered but rejected are listed with a reason. Where the question depends on a distinctive phrase, an exclusivity check records which records of the corpus contain that phrase (verified mechanically by verify_benchmark_11c.py against the in-memory corpus). Labels were NOT derived from retrieval ranks, model scores or any retrieval output on these questions, and no retriever was run on them.
differences_from_v2_guide: Strict labels use only the facet rule (a record is relevant when it contains the facet that the question asks about, for the same topic). The v2 cross-lane amendment (clause 1) is NOT applied to the strict labels.

Records of the other lane that the sources themselves declare as related and that describe the same behaviour are listed separately in lenient_extra_doc_ids. Evaluators may report a sensitivity analysis against strict union lenient; the strict set is primary.

The conjunction rule is kept: when a question asks for several things together, only records that contain all of them are relevant. Exclusivity checks were used to verify this against the full records, not a digest.
limitations: The author is an AI assistant of the same model family that wrote v1 and v2 and that implemented the retrievers; its judgement errors may be correlated with those of other AI reviewers.
The author knew the v1 and v2 questions and had seen retrieval results for v1 and v2 in earlier phases. It had not seen any result for these questions.
Several questions paraphrase a source sentence closely; they test whether a retriever finds a specific facet, not open-ended understanding.
Labels have not been independently reviewed, blind-annotated or checked by a human.

label_audit.note: Changes made to labels while authoring, found by the mechanical source checks in verify_benchmark_11c.py. All were made BEFORE the benchmark was frozen and BEFORE any retriever or embedding model was run on these questions. They are recorded here because this benchmark is not blind and the audit trail is part of its honesty.

changes.change: cwe:CWE-22 moved from lenient extra to strict relevant: its Potential Mitigations contain the same two pieces of advice (mapping fixed values to actual filenames; chroot jail) in different words. The question is restricted to path manipulation, so cwe:CWE-78 (similar generic advice, different topic) stays not relevant.
cwe:CWE-89 moved from lenient extra to strict relevant: its Potential Mitigations caution against dynamically constructing query strings inside stored procedures.
Exclusivity check scoped to the Alternate Terms section, because cwe:CWE-23 contains the words only inside a reference title. Strict label unchanged.

review_summary.note: Labels are single-pass author labels, grounded in verbatim source quotes. They are not blind, not independently annotated and not human-reviewed.

label_provenance.authored_by: AI assistant (Cursor agent), same model family as the authors of benchmark v1 and v2
label_provenance.labels_derived_from: source text of the 23 corpus records only

cases.question: Which weakness description warns that, because the application itself carries out the injected operating system commands, harmful activity may look as though it came from the application or its owner?

evidence.quote: any malicious activities may appear to come from the application or the application's owner

considered_not_relevant.reason: Generic command injection consequence mentions only an injected delimiter and a new command, not attribution to the application.
Attack pattern consequences list privilege gain and code execution without the attribution statement.

exclusivity_checks.phrase: appear to come from the application

The use of "Auth" as an abbreviation is discouraged, since it could be used for either authentication or authorization.

considered_not_relevant.reason: Authentication proves identity insufficiently; the secondary-channel scenario is not in this record.

cases.close_call: CAPEC-115 describes a related assumption about where authentication happens; excluded because the specific secondary-channel facet is only in CWE-306.

considered_not_relevant.reason: Code injection consequences concern server-side code, not scripts in a visitor's browser.

cases.question: Which advice limits outbound requests made on a user's behalf to the ordinary web protocols so that other URL schemes, such as local file access or file transfer, cannot be abused?
cases.task: Find the mitigation that restricts permitted URL schemas.
cases.rationale: Only the server-side request forgery attack pattern has mitigations, including restricting requests to HTTP or HTTPS so that schemes such as file:// and ftp:// are blocked.

considered_not_relevant.reason: Mentions file:// and other protocols as abuse in its consequences but has no mitigation advice (lenient extra only).

cases.question: Which mitigation advice for path manipulation says to use indirect references instead of actual file names, and also to run server interfaces under a non-root account or chroot-style jail?
cases.task: Find the mitigation list that contains both indirect references and a non-root or chroot confinement.
cases.rationale: For the path manipulation topic, the path traversal attack pattern and the path traversal weakness both give the two pieces of advice together: referencing files indirectly (CAPEC-126: indirect references; CWE-22: a mapping from fixed input values to the actual filenames) and confining the server (CAPEC-126: non-root account or chroot jail; CWE-22: a jail such as the Unix chroot jail, and lowest privileges). CWE-22 was added to the strict label after a source audit of paraphrased advice, before any retrieval was run (see label_audit).

evidence.quote: Use indirect references rather than actual file names.
Run server interfaces with a non-root account and/or utilize chroot jails
create a mapping from a set of fixed input values (such as numeric IDs) to the actual filenames or URLs, and reject all other inputs
OS-level examples include the Unix chroot jail, AppArmor, and SELinux.

considered_not_relevant.reason: Child weakness; its mitigations contain neither the mapping advice nor the jail advice (verified by exclusivity checks).
Has similar generic mapping and chroot jail advice, but for OS command injection, not for path manipulation, which the question restricts to.

exclusivity_checks.phrase: indirect references rather than actual file names
non-root account and/or utilize chroot jails
create a mapping from a set of fixed input values

cases.close_call: CWE-22 states the same advice in different words; it is included after the source audit. CWE-78 has similar generic advice but a different topic.

appending a new account at the end of a password file may allow an attacker to bypass authentication

SQL injection weakness; not about later command-line use.

cases.question: An intruder tried injected comparisons built from character codes to learn whether the backend was SQL Server or MySQL, judging only from whether the page answered normally. Which attack pattern describes identifying the database type this way?
cases.task: Find the attack pattern with a step that determines the database type using logical conditions.

evidence.quote: Determines the type of the database, such as MS SQL Server or Oracle or MySQL, using logical conditions as part of the injected queries

considered_not_relevant.reason: General SQL injection pattern; its execution flow has no database-type determination step.
Weakness record; no database fingerprinting step (lenient extra only as the declared related weakness of CAPEC-7).

exclusivity_checks.phrase: Determines the type of the database

cases.question: Which guidance cautions that stored procedures do not by themselves stop database query manipulation when the final statement is assembled dynamically?
cases.task: Find the mitigation that warns about dynamic query construction inside stored procedures.
cases.rationale: The SQL injection attack pattern says injection is possible even with stored procedures if the eventual query is constructed dynamically. The SQL injection weakness gives the same caution in other words: do not dynamically construct and execute query strings inside stored procedures, since that may re-introduce injection. CWE-89 was added to the strict label after a source audit of paraphrased advice, before any retrieval was run (see label_audit).

evidence.quote: Note that SQL Injection is possible even in the presence of stored procedures if the eventual query is constructed dynamically.
Do not dynamically construct and execute query strings within these features using "exec" or similar functionality, since this may re-introduce the possibility of SQL injection.

considered_not_relevant.reason: Blind SQL injection mitigations cover obscurity and input validation, not stored procedures.

exclusivity_checks.phrase: even in the presence of stored procedures

cases.close_call: The CWE-89 statement is a paraphrase of the CAPEC-66 caution; both are labelled relevant after the source audit.

cases.question: Why is hiding database error messages not enough to stop injection into queries, and what should an application do with errors instead?

considered_not_relevant.reason: Advises custom error pages that do not disclose database information, but does not state that suppressing errors is insufficient.

cases.close_call: CAPEC-66 gives overlapping custom-error-page advice; excluded under the conjunction rule because only CAPEC-7 states that suppression is insufficient.
